outcome: Since 26 January 2024 no accepted proof of the full statement is recorded, but on 6 October 2026 OpenAI released in its openai/math repository a 198-page manuscript (family 159) claiming a quasipolynomial-type density bound and, from it, the full reciprocal-sum statement for every length; a Lean chain for the reciprocal consequence exists in the repository, but no expert has verified the argument and the sources disagree on what the formal artifact establishes, while the only settled length (k=3) dates from 2020.
problem_asks: (i) Hypothesis: A is a set of positive integers whose reciprocals sum to infinity, i.e. the sum of 1/n over n in A diverges. (ii) Conclusion: A contains arithmetic progressions of every finite length k, that is 'arbitrarily long' read as: for each k there are a and d > 0 with a, a+d, ..., a+(k-1)d all in A (the Lean target reads the progressions as having positive common difference). (iii) The claim is universal over all such A and all k. It asks for existence of progressions, not for any quantitative bound, density threshold, or rate. The length-3 case, and sets such as the primes (whose reciprocal sum diverges), are instances of the universal claim, not separate parts. The 1936 Erdős-Turán density statement (sets of positive density contain 3-term APs) is a related but different question and is not what this bullet asks.

events.what_happened: Green and Tao proved that the primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions (arXiv math/0404188, 2004 per the search listing). The primes have a divergent reciprocal sum, so this is a special case of the conjecture, not the general statement. The Wikipedia article (fetched) describes it as a special case, including relatively dense subsets of the primes. I did not open the arXiv abstract page or confirm the journal publication.
events.delivers: The conjecture for A equal to the primes, and for relatively dense subsets of the primes (as the Wikipedia article describes). Restricted to that class of sets.
events.remains: The statement for every set of positive integers with a divergent reciprocal sum, for every length k, outside that prime-based class.
events.direction: Confirms the conjecture for the primes and dense subsets of the primes. Cuts in favour of the conjecture for that class; nothing contradicts it.

events.what_happened: Bloom and Sisask, 'Breaking the logarithmic barrier in Roth's theorem on arithmetic progressions' (arXiv 2007.03528, v1 7 July 2020; v2 1 Sept 2021). The arXiv abstract (opened) gives the density bound: a subset of {1..N} with no nontrivial 3-term AP has size at most about N/(log N)^(1+c). Quanta Magazine (3 Aug 2020, opened) reports that the result shows that a set whose reciprocals sum to infinity contains infinitely many evenly spaced triples, i.e. the length-3 case of the conjecture. The step from the density bound to the reciprocal statement is Quanta's description; I did not check it in the paper. Pre-window, recorded because it is the only length of the conjecture I found settled.
events.revisions: v1 7 Jul 2020; v2 1 Sep 2021 (current version per the arXiv abstract page).
events.delivers: The length-3 case: every set of positive integers with a divergent sum of reciprocals contains 3-term arithmetic progressions (Quanta: infinitely many evenly spaced triples). Restricted to length 3.
events.remains: Lengths k of 4 and above: the 'arbitrarily long' part of the statement is not reached.

events.what_happened: Kelley and Meka's bound for progression-free subsets of {1..N} with k = 3 (arXiv, Feb 2023 per the Wikipedia reference list; FOCS 2023 per the same list). The erdosproblems.com tag listing (opened) gives Erdős #140, 'Is r_3(N) ≪ N/(log N)^C for every C > 0?', as proved by Kelley and Meka. Bloom and Sisask later improved the exponent (arXiv 2309.02353, Sept 2023, per the Wikipedia reference list). The arXiv pages themselves were not opened; the months come from the Wikipedia summary.

events.remains: The reciprocal-sum statement for every length. This event does not move the problem as stated; the length-3 reciprocal case was already settled in 2020.

events.what_happened: Leng, Sah and Sawhney, 'Improved Bounds for Szemerédi's Theorem' (arXiv 2402.17995, v1 28 Feb 2024, v2 29 Feb 2024). For k at least 5 there is c_k > 0 with r_k(N) at most N times exp(-(log log N)^(c_k)), where r_k(N) is the largest subset of {1..N} with no k-term AP. Posted after the frozen revision. The abstract (opened) and the fetched text do not mention Erdős's reciprocal-sum conjecture. The value of c_k is not stated in what I read.
events.delivers: A density bound for k at least 5 on the neighbouring quantity r_k(N). Does not address divergent reciprocal sums in the text I read.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks. My own arithmetic (not from a source): a dyadic-block sum shows that a density bound of order (log N)^(-(1+e)) would make the reciprocal sum over a progression-free set converge, while exp(-(log log N)^c) with c below 1 does not. The text I read does not give c_k, so I cannot say whether this event reaches that threshold.
events.direction: Neighbouring density bound for k at least 5. Cuts neither way on the reciprocal-sum statement as far as the text I read shows.

events.what_happened: Rushil Raghavan, 'Improved Bounds for 3-Progressions' (arXiv, v1 27 Mar 2026; v2 1 May 2026; v3 15 May 2026, typo fixes). For 3-term-AP-free A in {1..N}, |A| is at most exp(-c (log N)^(1/6)/loglog N) times N, by iterating the Kelley-Meka sifting argument with a Bloom-Sisask bootstrapping step. The abstract (opened) does not mention reciprocal sums or the Erdős conjecture. The full text was not read.

events.remains: Everything in problem_asks. The length-3 reciprocal case was already settled in 2020.

It reviews the 1936 Erdős-Turán paper and Roth's work, progressions of length k at least 4, and open questions. Known only from the abstract and table of contents shown in search results; the article itself was not opened. Nothing new on the reciprocal-sum statement appears in what I saw.

events.what_happened: OpenAI's openai/math repository, family 159 ('Quasipolynomial bounds for arithmetic progressions'), contains a manuscript (folder dated 23 Sept 2026; 198 pages per Bloom and secondary coverage) and a Lean target. The manuscript's claims, as reported: (a) a quantitative density theorem for each fixed length k, which Bloom describes as progression-free subsets of {1..N} having size at most exp(-(log N)^(c_k)) times N for k at least 3; and (b) the reciprocal-sum statement, every set with a divergent sum of 1/n containing k-term APs for every k. In the Lean chain, (b) is derived from the density theorem, and Bloom reports that the Lean code appears to establish only a weaker density bound, exp(-(log log N)^(1+c_k)) times N. The repository's scope note says the formal statement excludes the quantitative bound. Bloom's post (8 Oct 2026, opened) lists Problem 3 among 23 Erdős-database items in the release, says the quantitative bound is much stronger than needed to imply the conjecture, and states that he has not examined any of the proofs seriously, has not checked that the Lean formalisations compile, and that the post is not an endorsement. Gasarch's blog (11 Oct 2026) states that OpenAI 'proved the entire conjecture' and that it is Lean-formalized; no check is described. Kalai's blog (7 Oct 2026) lists the item without assessment. Tao's blog carries an AHM statement of 7 Oct criticising the release; I did not read Tao's own posts on this result, and none of his titles addresses it.
events.revisions: The folder name dates the manuscript 23 Sept 2026. Outlets date the public repository release to Tuesday 6 Oct 2026; the repository page itself shows no release date. The repository's history.md has one dated entry (7 Oct 2026) on withdrawals, fixes and formalisations; it does not mention this family in the text I read. No arXiv version found.
events.delivers: If the manuscript and its Lean chain hold: the full reciprocal-sum statement for every length k, with APs of positive common difference (the formal def HasAP), via a density theorem. The density theorem is claimed in quasipolynomial form (Bloom's description) but the formal chain is reported to use a weaker bound, exp(-(log log N)^(1+c_k)) times N, which by my own dyadic check (not from a source) is still enough to make the reciprocal sum converge. Restriction: the formal theorem statement does not contain the quantitative bound.
events.remains: Nothing of problem_asks if the claim holds. Not verified: whether the 198-page density argument is correct; whether the formal chain is free of sorry across its full import closure; whether the formal density definition is the weaker bound Bloom reports (it is defined in an imported module I did not read); whether the reduction lemma's hypotheses match the manuscript's theorem.

The config names solution module OAI.Combinatorics.Progressions.Main (imports only, as read) and the allowed axioms propext, Quot.sound, Classical.choice. Results/Conclusions.lean proves manuscriptReciprocalProgressionTheorem as the second projection of manuscript_main_theorems : QuantitativeDensityTheorem and ReciprocalProgressionTheorem. Estimates/UniformRelativePatchSource.lean contains a lemma reciprocalProgressionTheorem_of_quantitativeDensityTheorem and a lemma eventually_exp_loglog_rpow_le; I read no sorry, admit, axiom or native_decide in the five solution-chain files I read (Conclusions, Geometry/Erdos3AllocatedZeroLayerDetectionTransport, Estimates/UniformRelativePatchSource, Results/FullLibrary, Main). The definitions of QuantitativeDensityTheorem and ReciprocalProgressionTheorem and the remaining imported modules were not read. These checks used a summarising fetch, not a compiler or a grep. formalization.yaml lists status 'Partial progress' and review 'unchecked'. No Comparator run result was found.

events.directly_checkable: The openai/math Lean project can be compiled, and ErdosReciprocal.json run through Comparator; I did not run it. The 198-page PDF could not be read through my tools (binary stream), so the density argument was not checked.
events.doubts: (1) Scope of the formal result: the repository scope note excludes the quantitative bound from the formal statement, and Bloom reports the Lean code appears to prove a weaker bound; the headline bound is therefore not formally checked. (2) Verification status: formalization.yaml says review 'unchecked'; OpenAI's README says 'Some of the unformalized results could have issues'; Bloom says he has not examined the proofs. (3) Substance: a secondary analysis reported via search summary describes the paper as using essentially all existing techniques in the area, so the claimed gain would come from combining them; and the claimed bound is much stronger than the best known for k at least 4 (per Bloom). No expert reading of the 198-page argument appears in the sources. (4) Provenance: per the README and press reports, each result came from a single prompt to an unreleased internal model with about three hours of compute, and prompts were not published. (5) Reported but unverified: OpenAI disabled GitHub Issues on the repository (one outlet only). Earlier OpenAI Erdős claims were judged by Bloom to be 'a dramatic misrepresentation' (Oct 2025), a different result. These are signals, not a verdict.
events.direction: Cuts in favour of the conjecture: claims a proof of it for every length k, through a density theorem stronger than the conjecture needs. Not a counterexample.

events.what_happened: The manuscript 'Quasipolynomial Bounds for Arithmetic Progressions' (OpenAI, dated September 23, 2026) states as its first claim that it proves Erdős's conjecture: every set of positive integers with divergent reciprocal sum contains arithmetic progressions of every finite length. Its Corollary 'Divergent reciprocal sums' says that every A ⊆ ℕ with Σ_{a∈A} 1/a = ∞ contains nonconstant arithmetic progressions of every finite length. The corollary is derived from the main Theorem: for each fixed k ≥ 3 there are constants Cₖ, cₖ, εₖ > 0 such that, for every N ≥ 2, rₖ(N) ≤ Cₖ·N·exp(−cₖ(log N)^εₖ), where rₖ(N) is the largest subset of {1,…,N} with no nonconstant k-term progression (common difference d > 0). The proof sums the density bound over dyadic blocks [2^m, 2^(m+1)), using that a progression-free A meets each block in at most rₖ(2^m) elements, and shows the reciprocal sum is finite. Lengths one and two follow from A being infinite. The same manuscript also proves a weighted version: Σ (log(2+a))^B / a = ∞ for any fixed B ≥ 0 forces progressions of every length (Corollary 'Logarithmic weights and every length'), and it recovers Green and Tao's theorem on dense subsets of the primes.
events.delivers: Claims the list's question in full as stated: for every set of positive integers with divergent reciprocal sum, and for every finite length, there is a nonconstant arithmetic progression of that length, with positive common difference. The abstract says outright 'We prove Erdős's conjecture', and the manuscript's statement matches the list's hypothesis (Σ 1/a = ∞ over the set) and conclusion (arbitrarily long progressions, read as every finite length). No density, class or dimension restriction is attached to the corollary. Sets such as the primes are instances of the universal claim. The density bound behind it is quantitative but the corollary needs only its summability consequence.
events.remains: Nothing in the list's statement, if the claim is correct. The quantitative density question is not closed: the bound is stretched-exponential in log N with an unspecified exponent εₖ and is stated as not optimized, and the manuscript makes no claim about the exact size of rₖ(N).

machine_checked.scope:
Erdős's reciprocal-sum conjecture asks whether every set of positive integers with divergent reciprocal sum contains arithmetic progressions of every finite length. The formalization proves this statement: for every requested length, such a set contains a progression with positive common difference.

The selected theorem is the reciprocal-sum consequence. The paper's quantitative upper bound for the largest progression-free subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ is outside this statement.

events.doubts: (1) No constant is given a value. Cₖ, cₖ, εₖ and Aₖ are asserted to exist for each k, and the text says the exponent is not optimized. (2) The central new estimate, that the width loss at weight h is bounded by a polynomial independent of the current width Q_h, is argued in Section 8 through a four-step parameter schedule and two propositions. The polynomials Fⱼ, Gⱼ, Pⱼ and P'ᵢ are asserted to exist rather than written out, and several steps defer to other sections ('as in Section …'). The key justification reads 'Every step in the descending schedule uses a bounded composition of polynomial logarithmic bounds'. (3) In the root-compression lemma the radii are chosen 'with equality up to fixed factors'. (4) The corollary says 'nonconstant' progressions of every finite length, but a one-term progression cannot be nonconstant. The text handles lengths one and two by infinitude, so the statement is in effect for k ≥ 2. (5) I checked the statements of the appendix results and the places where the main text cites them, not their proofs; the foundations appendices run to about 10,000 lines.; conditional on: The main density bound is proved in the manuscript from external inputs it cites rather than proves. The two principal ones, named in the introduction, are the quasipolynomial inverse theorem for the Gowers U^(s+1)[N] norm of Leng, Sah and Sawhney (arXiv:2402.17994, Theorem 1.2; the appendices also cite its Lemma B.5 and Theorem 5.4 with Corollary 5.5), and the radius-sensitive almost-periodicity theorem of Schoen and Sisask (arXiv:1408.2568, Theorem 5.4), restated in the manuscript as its Lemma 'Almost-periodicity with a width bound'. Other cited inputs include Leng's efficient equidistribution theorem (Theorem 4), Green–Tao results on polynomial orbits (Proposition 7.2 and Lemma 7.4), Conlon–Fox–Zhao densification, and Bergelson–Leibman. The manuscript says it proves the box and product-of-cyclic-groups extensions of the Leng–Sah–Sawhney interval theorem itself. The corollary depends on the main theorem of this same manuscript. It does not depend on the companion van der Waerden manuscript, which is cited only for a coloring remark.

disputes.summary: Whether the formal chain establishes the conjecture or only a weaker density bound. OpenAI's Lean scope note (159.md) says the formalization 'proves this statement' (the reciprocal-sum consequence) and excludes the quantitative bound. Bloom says the Lean code 'appears to prove the weaker bound' exp(-(log log N)^(1+c_k)) times N, and that the Comparator challenge file has only the statement. Gasarch says OpenAI 'proved the entire conjecture' and that it is Lean-formalized. The solution-chain files I read are consistent with a reduction from a density theorem; the density definition lies in an imported module I did not read. The sources do not resolve this.

Verification status is contested in tone rather than in fact. Gasarch treats the result as proved and says 'I hope it soon becomes people-understood'. Bloom says he has not checked it and that his post is not an endorsement. Kalai lists it without assessment. OpenAI's README says some unformalized results 'could have issues'. Tao's public criticism concerns the release as a whole ('AI prompters' per TechCrunch, unverified in primary form), not this result.

summary: The problem is the Erdős-Turán / Erdős reciprocal-sum conjecture, Erdős problem #3 on erdosproblems.com (statement and $5000 prize confirmed on the live page I read, which was last edited 4 April 2026 and shows 'Proof claims (0)'). Before the window, two results touch it: Green and Tao (2004) for the primes, a special case; and Bloom and Sisask (2020), whose density bound settles the length-3 case, per Quanta. Kelley and Meka (2023), and Bloom and Sisask's follow-up, improve the length-3 density bound, a neighbouring quantity. In the window after 26 January 2024 the human work I found is neighbouring: Leng, Sah and Sawhney (28 Feb 2024) bound r_k(N) for k at least 5 with an exponent c_k whose value I could not read; Raghavan (27 Mar 2026) improves the length-3 density bound; and Green's 2026 JLMS survey is expository. The decisive event is OpenAI's family 159 in the openai/math repository, released 6 Oct 2026 (manuscript folder dated 23 Sept 2026, 198 pages): a quantitative density theorem and the reciprocal-sum consequence. Bloom (8 Oct) says the claimed bound is far stronger than the conjecture needs. Sources disagree on what the Lean establishes (see disputes). What I could check: the comparator target file proves the statement only by sorry, as expected; the solution chain (Results/Conclusions.lean) derives the reciprocal theorem from a conjunction whose first component is QuantitativeDensityTheorem; Estimates/UniformRelativePatchSource.lean contains the reduction lemma and an eventually_exp_loglog_rpow_le lemma, which fits Bloom's description of a weaker exp(-(log log N)^(1+c_k)) bound. That weaker bound is still sufficient for convergence of the reciprocal sum by my own dyadic calculation (not from a source). formalization.yaml gives 'Partial progress' and review 'unchecked'. No expert has reviewed the 198-page argument in the sources. Bloom explicitly did not check it. Gasarch, a blogger, reports it as proved. The erdosproblems.com/3 snapshot I read predates the release, so its status line is not updated; Bloom's post says Problem 3 is among the 23 items. ProofAtlas (status checked 14 Aug 2026; an AI-first platform, not a referee) labels the problem 'partially resolved' before the release; that is its own claim and I did not verify it. AI involvement: the OpenAI README names only 'an internal OpenAI model' (pre-release, unreleased, not named). It describes the collection as produced by that model, so the involvement is claimed to be load-bearing, but the README does not name family 159 individually. Compute is given as about three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking per result. No human authors are named in the pages I could read. Source caveats: the Wikipedia fetch summary says the article was last edited on 12 October 2026, which is after today's date (11 October 2026), so I treat its summary as unreliable, including its claim that the article now mentions the OpenAI proof. The fetch tool summarises pages with a small model, so quotes obtained that way are not verbatim checks, and I say so where it matters, notably the sorry check. One Bloom forum comment on thread 3 (Sept 2025) concerns a different variant and is not recorded as an event. The Epoch FrontierMath Erdős benchmark (launched 1 Sept 2026, 68 problems open as of Aug 2026) may include Problem 3; I could not confirm it from the page.
competing_reading: Strong reading: the Lean chain proves the full conjecture from a density theorem weaker than the headline bound, the formal statements match the problem, and the problem is settled as of October 2026 pending checks; Bloom's concern is about the quantitative bound, which the conjecture does not need. Weak reading: the only formal artifact states the conjecture with a sorry; the proof rests on an unreviewed 198-page PDF from an unnamed internal model with no human authors named; Bloom did not check it; the formal density definition and the full import closure were not read; so no accepted proof exists and the problem remains open in the sense that counts for a judging pass.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A readable copy of the 198-page density argument and its reduction to the conjecture, and a written check by a named expert (Bloom, Green, Kelley, Meka, Sisask, or others) of the key density step. (2) A Comparator or lake build of the openai/math Lean project with a grep for sorry, admit, axiom and native_decide over the full import closure, plus the definitions of QuantitativeDensityTheorem and ReciprocalProgressionTheorem, which would show whether the formal density bound is the weak or the strong form. (3) The live erdosproblems.com/3 status and forum thread after 8 Oct 2026. (4) Evidence whether the family appears on the withdrawn or corrected list in the repository history. (5) For the LSS 2024 result, the value of c_k, to test whether it crosses the threshold.

event.what_happened: OpenAI's openai/math repository, family 159 ('Quasipolynomial bounds for arithmetic progressions'), contains a manuscript (folder dated 23 Sept 2026; 198 pages per Bloom and secondary coverage) and a Lean target. The manuscript's claims, as reported: (a) a quantitative density theorem for each fixed length k, which Bloom describes as progression-free subsets of {1..N} having size at most exp(-(log N)^(c_k)) times N for k at least 3; and (b) the reciprocal-sum statement, every set with a divergent sum of 1/n containing k-term APs for every k. In the Lean chain, (b) is derived from the density theorem, and Bloom reports that the Lean code appears to establish only a weaker density bound, exp(-(log log N)^(1+c_k)) times N. The repository's scope note says the formal statement excludes the quantitative bound. Bloom's post (8 Oct 2026, opened) lists Problem 3 among 23 Erdős-database items in the release, says the quantitative bound is much stronger than needed to imply the conjecture, and states that he has not examined any of the proofs seriously, has not checked that the Lean formalisations compile, and that the post is not an endorsement. Gasarch's blog (11 Oct 2026) states that OpenAI 'proved the entire conjecture' and that it is Lean-formalized; no check is described. Kalai's blog (7 Oct 2026) lists the item without assessment. Tao's blog carries an AHM statement of 7 Oct criticising the release; I did not read Tao's own posts on this result, and none of his titles addresses it.
event.revisions: The folder name dates the manuscript 23 Sept 2026. Outlets date the public repository release to Tuesday 6 Oct 2026; the repository page itself shows no release date. The repository's history.md has one dated entry (7 Oct 2026) on withdrawals, fixes and formalisations; it does not mention this family in the text I read. No arXiv version found.
event.delivers: If the manuscript and its Lean chain hold: the full reciprocal-sum statement for every length k, with APs of positive common difference (the formal def HasAP), via a density theorem. The density theorem is claimed in quasipolynomial form (Bloom's description) but the formal chain is reported to use a weaker bound, exp(-(log log N)^(1+c_k)) times N, which by my own dyadic check (not from a source) is still enough to make the reciprocal sum converge. Restriction: the formal theorem statement does not contain the quantitative bound.
event.remains: Nothing of problem_asks if the claim holds. Not verified: whether the 198-page density argument is correct; whether the formal chain is free of sorry across its full import closure; whether the formal density definition is the weaker bound Bloom reports (it is defined in an imported module I did not read); whether the reduction lemma's hypotheses match the manuscript's theorem.

event.doubts: (1) Scope of the formal result: the repository scope note excludes the quantitative bound from the formal statement, and Bloom reports the Lean code appears to prove a weaker bound; the headline bound is therefore not formally checked. (2) Verification status: formalization.yaml says review 'unchecked'; OpenAI's README says 'Some of the unformalized results could have issues'; Bloom says he has not examined the proofs. (3) Substance: a secondary analysis reported via search summary describes the paper as using essentially all existing techniques in the area, so the claimed gain would come from combining them; and the claimed bound is much stronger than the best known for k at least 4 (per Bloom). No expert reading of the 198-page argument appears in the sources. (4) Provenance: per the README and press reports, each result came from a single prompt to an unreleased internal model with about three hours of compute, and prompts were not published. (5) Reported but unverified: OpenAI disabled GitHub Issues on the repository (one outlet only). Earlier OpenAI Erdős claims were judged by Bloom to be 'a dramatic misrepresentation' (Oct 2025), a different result. These are signals, not a verdict.
event.direction: Cuts in favour of the conjecture: claims a proof of it for every length k, through a density theorem stronger than the conjecture needs. Not a counterexample.

judgement.why: The statement asks only for the reciprocal-sum implication for every length. Green-Tao (primes) and Bloom-Sisask (k=3) are pre-snapshot cases. Kelley-Meka, Leng-Sah-Sawhney and Raghavan bound r_k(N), a neighbouring density quantity that is not the statement's question; LSS's bound exp(-(log log N)^c_k) is not shown to reach the summability threshold, so these are variant. Green's survey is expository (none). The two OpenAI rows describe one release (the research pass and the repository stage); both claim the full statement via a dyadic summation of a density theorem, so scope whole. Nobody named has worked through the argument (Bloom explicitly did not; Gasarch only repeats the claim) and a Lean build is not digestion, so unreviewed. Doubtful rather than not_credible: there is no identified error and the reduction step is standard, but the headline density bound would be a major leap and the formal chain's content is disputed. AI role generated per the repository's own statement that the manuscripts were produced by the model; no human authors are named.
judgement.doubts: The two OpenAI events are duplicates of one release (dated 6 Oct 2026). The README attributes production to the model at collection level rather than naming family 159 individually. Bloom-Sisask's k=3 consequence for reciprocal sums rests on Quanta's description; verification left unreviewed since no named expert reading or journal acceptance is in the record.
